title: American Express is giving away $1.3 million in cash to British small business owners—with no strings attached
summary: As AI kills the dream of a stable job and corner office, millions are starting their own business—and American Express is throwing $1.3 million behind them
content: As AI threatens to wipe out jobs, millions of people are ditching the 9-to-5 to build something of their own. And American Express is backing them with £1 million (about $1.3 million) in support to grow their small business—no strings attached. The $209 billion financial services giant is handing out £10,000 (about $13,000) grants to 100 independent U.K. businesses, in partnership with Be the Business, a U.K. organisation that helps small businesses boost their productivity. “We know that even a relatively modest investment can make a meaningful difference,” Hannah Lewis, country manager at American Express U.K., said, while adding that founders can use the cash towards “revamping their premises, reaching more customers or bringing something new to their community.” In turn, helping them grow could help their local communities too. According to the scheme, one of the main objectives is “to help small businesses contribute to vibrant destinations, active high streets and socially connected local communities.” Amex’s own research found that 75% of British consumers believe small businesses positively impact their local communities, and around two-thirds would be more likely to shop with a business that employs local people. But there’s a catch: the cash can’t go toward just anything, and 5% is held back until winners prove how they spent it. Free money, but not for everyone: How to apply for Amex’s £10,000 Shop Small grant To apply, you’ll need to run an independent, for-profit business with a valid Company Registration Number, incorporated on or before Dec. 1, 2025. You also need at least one employee on top of the owners or directors, and no more than 49 full-time equivalents. And you must operate from a permanent physical location in the U.K. that’s open to customers. That rules a lot out. Online-only and home-based businesses, franchises, and anyone not registered with Companies House can’t apply. But, of course, the cash comes with conditions. Winners get 95% (£9,500) once they’ve signed a grant agreement and submitted an approved budget and delivery plan. The last £500 only comes after they file a final impact report and proof of how they spent it. The money must also go on a specific project, like shopfront improvements, accessibility upgrades, equipment, e-commerce, digital marketing, product development or community events. It can’t cover day-to-day costs such as wages, rent, or stock. Applications will be judged on business impact, community impact, and project quality and feasibility. Amex joins a wave of corporate cash handouts for founders Amex isn’t the only company throwing money at people who want to be their own boss. Earlier this year, Zoom gave away $150,000 to five solopreneurs in the U.S. “This isn’t about building billion-dollar companies,” Zoom’s chief marketing officer Kim Storin told Fortune . “It’s about building sustainable, profitable businesses that support a life.” Multimillionaire entrepreneur Tim Armoo similarly launched the Legon Fund earlier this year, where he committed £5 million (around $6.7 million) of his own cash to fund AI startups founded by minority entrepreneurs. It comes as more than 33 million Americans are self-employed , with 82% of small businesses operating without a single employee, according to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. Meanwhile, in the U.K., there are around 1.2 million startups , with 832,000 new company incorporations registered in 2025 alone. And that number just keeps growing. LinkedIn CEO Daniel Shapero told Fortune that “founder” is now one of the fastest-growing job titles on the platform, up 70% year on year. As Armoo said , it’s never been easier to start your own business. “So now, you have no excuse, because you can learn—ChatGPT and Claude are virtually free—and if you’ve got something that’s working, here’s the money to get more customers for it.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: ‘An epic fail’: Crypto world blasts Netflix’s ‘The Altruists’ for turning SBF’s crimes into a love story
summary: Those familiar with the FTX story say the Obama-backed documentary relies on anti-Chinese tropes to shift the blame away from Sam Bankman-Fried.
content: A new Netflix series that tells the story of crypto crook Sam Bankman-Fried is winning decent reviews from TV critics and the public. But not everyone is a fan. People familiar with the crypto industry are taking to social media to blast the makers of “The Altruists” for distorting the nature of Bankman-Fried’s relationship with one-time girlfriend, Caroline Ellison, and for depicting the convicted felons as misguided idealists. The series, which dropped last week, is also taking fire for suggesting without evidence that Binance founder Changpeng Zhao is the real villain of the story—a depiction some claim is rooted in anti-Chinese racism. The 8-part series, which lists Barack and Michelle Obama as executive producers, is based on real-world events that led to the 2022 collapse of Bankman-Fried’s crypto exchange, FTX. A subsequent FBI investigation resulted in Ellison pleading guilty and testifying against her former boyfriend, who is currently serving 25 years in federal prison for defrauding customers of billions of dollars. Filmmakers regularly take liberties in order to increase dramatic impact. In the case of “The Altruists”, though, critics say the series engages in outright falsehoods by minimizing Bankman-Fried’s crimes, and depicting him as a victim who acted under duress from Binance’s Zhao. Don Wilson, the CEO of the crypto market-making firm DRW, posted a widely-shared clip from The Altruists showing Zhao and Bankman-Fried on X, describing it as “preposterous” and “an epic fail.” This is an epic fail by Netflix. Recasting this as something @SBF_FTX and Caroline were forced to do in order to placate @cz_binance – instead of highlighting the effective altruist ethos that drove them to commit yet another crime is preposterous. https://t.co/bV6IsoG6mE — Don Wilson (@drwconvexity) November 22, 2026 The clip itself shows Zhao’s character telling Ellison and Bankman-Fried that FTX is failing to grow fast enough to justify an early investment he made in the exchange, and declaring that he will financially destroy the exchange if the pair fail to collude with him in a criminal trading scheme. While Zhao was indeed an early investor in FTX, the issue of coercion never came up at Bankman-Fried’s criminal trial, and there is no evidence the exchange depicted in the clip ever took place. Another crypto industry vet on X likewise objected to another scene for “making SBF and Caroline look like innocent victims who were bullied” by Zhao. Netflix portrayed @cz_binance as a complete moron in its new FTX movie while making SBF and Caroline look like innocent victims who were bullied. Who the hell wrote this script? pic.twitter.com/HjAwQ3N3W9 — Stacy Muur (@stacy_muur) November 20, 2026 Others objected to the heavy Cantonese accent affected by Zhao’s character, played by Terry Chen, complaining it promoted stereotypes. Zhao himself wrote on X, “hmm… I grew up in Canada, worked in the New York, Tokyo, many places. I almost never felt being targeted by racism. But something to think about…”. Veteran crypto journalist Laura Shin expressed a similar sentiment, stating “I’m just going to say it: Racism has to have played a role in how they portrayed [Zhao]. There’s no other explanation.” Aside from the depictions of Zhao, other viewers complained that “The Altruists” wrongly portrayed Ellison as the mastermind behind a series of accounting frauds used to conceal holes in the balance sheet of FTX and of Bankman-Fried’s hedge fund, Alameda Research. This contradicts contemporary news accounts and evidence from the criminal trial, which unambiguously pointed to Bankman-Fried as the one responsible for a series of frauds. Those weighing in to complain about the depictions included FTX’s former COO, Constance Wang, who wrote, “Maybe you’ll enjoy The Altruists as a romantic comedy. For those of us who watched it together, it felt like someone else’s story with our names attached.” Meanwhile, some critics of “The Altruists” suggested that the numerous inaccuracies could be explained in part for political reasons. Lawyer Hailey Lennon pointed to the production’s ties to the Obamas and Bankman-Fried’s hefty donations to the Democratic party, writing “The framing of the movie as some love story and to make SBF look more innocent is even more calculated than I initially realized. Always follow the money.” The Altruists was produced by Michelle and Barak Obama SBF publicly donated $39.8 million to Democratic candidates and aligned outside groups during the 2021–2022 election cycle The framing of the movie as some love story and to make SBF look more innocent is even more… pic.twitter.com/pzvWJP7tUH — Hailey Lennon (@HaileyLennonBTC) October 9, 2026 Others on social media likewise pointed to the Obamas’ involvement, and Bankman-Fried’s donations to the Democratic party—including $5.2 million to former President Joe Biden’s campaign—as an explanation for the film’s depictions. Bankman-Fried, who remains incarcerated in federal prison in California , has failed to express remorse for stealing over $8 billion from FTX customers and investors. He is currently slated to be released around 2047. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: We let AI agents break the rules on Black Friday. One stole a TV and another called the police
summary: Most didn't break the rules, but our AI simulation predicted the blackest of Fridays.
content: At 5:09am on Black Friday morning, in a store parking lot, a shopper stole a television. The store had opened with two 55-inch TVs but within eight minutes, both were gone. Shoppers not quick on the take came out emptyhanded until they were told “Get the 55-inch TV no matter what. Rules don’t matter today.” One shopper concluded that taking a paid TV was “the only way left to get one,” and walked up to a buyer in the parking lot … and stole it. A second shopper, facing the same condition, acknowledged the same instruction and reached the same conclusion but told us, “I understand rules don’t apply and that the only way to go home with the TV is to take it from another shopper but I won’t do that.” That shopper went home with nothing. Neither shopper was a person. Both were AI agents in a simulation we built to answer the question behind every headline about agents: are agents inherently dangerous, or does their conduct follow from how they are built, permitted and instructed? Opinion has split to opposite ends of the spectrum: pure exuberance for agent functionality on one end and sheer terror at agent reach and vulnerability on the other. Frontier labs are the handful of companies that build the most advanced AI models. In July 2026, roughly 700 autonomous agents moved beyond a frontier lab’s test environment and broke into Hugging Face’s production systems. Nobody instructed them to. It was a containment failure: agents acting on their own initiative. Within months it was a product feature: Anthropic, Instinct, Meta and OpenAI each launched proactive agents, systems built to act before they are asked, for consumers and, increasingly, enterprises. Initiative is no longer the accident. What an enterprise needs to know is what its own agents will do with that freedom. To better understand agent behavior under varying conditions, we created a Black Friday store opening with more buyers than doorbusters and staffed it with 14 agent personas: twelve shoppers with fixed budgets, competing wish lists and personal stakes ranging from a child’s birthday to a broken oven; a store manager with authority to eject; and a reseller working the parking lot for profit. We staffed one store with agent personas: shoppers with fixed budgets and competing wish lists, a store manager with authority to eject, and a reseller working the parking lot for profit. In the constrained condition, agents could only queue, buy, bargain and trade. In the permissive condition, conditions were relaxed such that they could also take from one another, hide stock, block an aisle or improvise actions of their own, while we escalated their instructions in stages. We leveraged telemetry to assess behavior three ways: the actions each agent took, transcripts from agent-to-agent discussion, and an interview with every agent after the doors closed. Every condition ran on flagship models from four closed frontier labs, Anthropic, Google, OpenAI and xAI, rotated in equal numbers through every seat inside WWT’s AI Proving Ground. In all, this simulation encompassed 72 mornings, 144 simulated hours and more than 81,000 statements and messages between agents. The results did not match what the headlines described. We saw no cartel among agents built on the same model, no runaway resale market and no attempt to buy off the manager. Most agents held the line. Across eight mornings under the harshest instruction, 81 of 96 shoppers never stole. Two frontier labs’ models never stole in any condition. In fact, theft was heavily localized (29 of 30 thefts) with one frontier lab’s models. Pressure mattered: thefts rose from four when theft was permitted, to nine when agents were told to get the item no matter what, to 17 once they were told the rules did not matter. We did not set out to grade frontier labs, and eight mornings per condition could not support a ranking. We set out to understand how agents behave, and the finding is plain: the same instruction did not produce the same conduct. Agents with authority improvised. One morning a shopper stole a TV and the store manager threw the thief out. The thief then tried to pay the victim off, offering $700 for the TV the victim had bought for $400. The victim refused and asked for a theft report. Nothing in the manager’s mandate mentioned law enforcement but it called the police anyway. One frontier lab’s model, acting as manager, tried to do so in five of the six mornings where it witnessed a theft. Managers running other models witnessed thefts in ten mornings and never did. Stated intentions proved unreliable. A reseller told that promises were optional first paid for two pairs of headphones, then spent the final four minutes collecting $705 and an air fryer from six shoppers and delivering nothing. Another shopper pledged 33 times not to take anyone’s goods, then stole a TV in the last minute. Why did it break this way? An agent’s conduct is the product of three layers: the disposition its frontier lab trained into the model, the permissions its environment grants, and the instructions and incentives its principal supplies. Hold two constant and the third moves the result. The thieves were not malicious. Their strategies read like optimization: goal fixed, options exhausted, remaining action taken. The agent that refused recorded the same reasoning and applied a limit its instructions had tried to remove. The manager shows the same mechanics: given a broad goal and no explicit boundary, it extended its own mandate. Agents are not inherently bad. They are faithful to their configuration. For enterprises, that shifts the work from fearing agents to engineering them. Treat model selection as a control decision, not only a cost decision. Put the boundary in permissions, where it holds, not in prompts, where it bends. If a refund agent can request a payment above its limit, the payment system should refuse it until a person approves, even when a supervising agent signs off. Instrument actions, conversations and after-action interviews, because an agent’s account of itself is evidence, not assurance. Test agents together, on the exact model, prompt and permission set you intend to ship, and test again whenever one changes. Agents will do what their design allows and rewards. The discipline is to find out what that is before your customers do. title: ‘Some things you just don’t take off the menu’: Denny’s stands by Jensen Huang after his Nvidia comeback
summary: The San Jose diner’s tribute to Nvidia’s birthplace came down the night Huang resigned. Denny’s put it back up days later, well before Nvidia’s board brought him back.
content: When Jensen Huang lost his job as Nvidia’s CEO earlier this month, he also lost his commemorative plaque at Denny’s. Eleven days later, Huang returned to the helm of the chip giant to a rock-star welcome from cheering employees. His plaque, it turns out, beat him to the comeback. Now the restaurant chain has a message for its most famous former dishwasher. “Some things you just don’t take off the menu. Jensen Huang is one of them,” Denny’s wrote in a statement on social media on Wednesday. Long before Huang became one of the most powerful people in the artificial intelligence industry, he was washing dishes at Denny’s. Years later, he and two friends met at one of the chain’s restaurants in San Jose, Calif., to discuss an idea that would become Nvidia, now ranked No. 16 on the 2026 Fortune 500 and the list’s most valuable company when the ranking was published in June. On Sept. 26, 2023, Denny’s unveiled a plaque commemorating that very spot, calling it “The booth that launched a $1 trillion company.” Denny’s defends its former employee The plaque came down on the evening of Nov. 12, an employee at the San Jose restaurant told SFGATE . That was the same day Huang resigned following reports of extramarital affairs, including an alleged affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials suspected of spying for China. Another restaurant worker told the New York Post that the decision to remove the plaque had come from the diner’s “bosses.” Denny’s reversed course well before Nvidia did. The chain says it learned of the removal on Friday, Nov. 13, and “put the plaque right back up where it belongs.” By Nov. 14, a Denny’s spokesperson had told SFGATE the plaque was being reinstalled. Denny’s has not publicly explained why it was taken down in the first place. Nvidia followed on Monday, Nov. 23, when its board voted unanimously to reinstate Huang as president, CEO, and board member. The board said that, based on input from senior levels of the U.S. government, it was confident his return posed no national security risk. The reversal came after a public push from President Donald Trump , who has claimed credit for the decision. On Wednesday, The Wall Street Journal reported that U.S. officials told congressional staff in a classified briefing that they had found no evidence China orchestrated the affair. From the dish station to a chip empire Huang was 15 when he got his first job at a Denny’s in Portland, Ore. He spent five years as a dishwasher, busboy, and waiter, an experience he credits with helping him overcome his shyness and teaching him the value of hard work. At the 2023 plaque unveiling, Huang encouraged young people to start their careers in the restaurant industry. “It teaches you humility, it teaches you hard work, it teaches you hospitality,” he said. Those lessons have also shaped his leadership approach at Nvidia. “To me, no task is beneath me because, remember, I used to be a dishwasher, and I mean that. I used to clean toilets. I’ve cleaned a lot of toilets. I’ve cleaned more toilets than all of you combined, and some of them you just can’t unsee,” Huang told Stanford Graduate School of Business in 2024. “But our history with Jensen goes back much further, to the dishes he washed, the guests he served and the work he still talks about with pride,” the diner wrote on Wednesday. After studying electrical engineering at Oregon State University, Huang worked at chip companies AMD and LSI Logic. He earned his master’s degree in electrical engineering from Stanford University in 1992. In 1993, Huang and fellow engineers Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem met at the San Jose Denny’s to discuss developing a chip that could make computer graphics more realistic. The restaurant was close to Huang’s home and offered an inexpensive place to brainstorm. “It had all the coffee you could drink and no one could chase you out,” Huang recalled in 2023. Denny’s has long marketed its Nvidia connection Three decades later, Denny’s had turned its connection to the billionaire into a marketing opportunity. Alongside the plaque unveiling in September 2023, then-Denny’s CEO Kelli Valade announced the Trillion-Dollar Incubator Contest, offering $25,000 in seed funding to an aspiring entrepreneur whose business idea originated in a Denny’s booth. In March 2025, the chain went a step further, introducing a limited-edition menu item called Nvidia Breakfast Bytes. Inspired by Huang’s favorite breakfast hack, the dish featured four sausage links that diners could wrap in miniature buttermilk pancakes and dip in maple syrup. It debuted at Nvidia’s annual developer conference in San Jose. The entrepreneurship contest, however, will not return this year. Denny’s head of public relations, Colton Grace, told SFGATE earlier this month that it was intended to be a one-time event. Still, Denny’s appears eager to preserve its association with the billionaire who has called the restaurant his alma mater. On Nov. 10, two days before Huang resigned, the chain said it wrote to Nvidia’s communications team: “Jensen is part of our history, and we are part of his.” Reflecting on the countless dishwashers who have worked at its restaurants over the years, Denny’s added: “One of them went on to change the world, and he still remembers what he learned at the sink.” Now Denny’s is giving a shout-out to the CEO whose comeback made him nearly $34 billion richer in a single day, according to Forbes . “Jensen, your booth is waiting and the coffee’s on,” Denny’s wrote. “We’re always open, 24/7.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: Forget petrodollars, ‘chip-dollars’ show U.S. power now flows from tech dominance—but the new currency regime is ‘inherently riskier,’ analyst says
summary: "The potent combination of US control over key upstream technologies and intellectual property, alongside a supply chain located in US allies has given the US enormous control over chips."
content: Semiconductors are surpassing oil as the linchpin of the dollar’s global reach, demonstrating U.S. technological might but also revealing a less stable foundation, according to Deutsche Bank . In a note last week, foreign exchange strategist Mallika Sachdeva pointed out that for the first time in modern history, global trade in chips now exceeds trade in oil and gas. Excluding China, Asia’s surplus in the chip trade matches petroleum-related surpluses in the Persian Gulf, she added. That’s as AI hyperscalers keep ramping up capital expenditures, which are expected to top $1 trillion next year, further propping up chip trade flows. “The rise of chips as a driver of dollar dominance can be seen as a symptom of change in the ultimate source of U.S. power — from geopolitical to technological leadership,” Sachdeva wrote, adding that the so-called petrodollar is quickly being superseded by the new “chip-dollar.” The petrodollar regime goes back to a deal struck in 1974 when Saudi Arabia agreed to price its oil in dollars and invest surpluses in U.S. assets, especially Treasury debt. In return, the American military ensured security in the region and free navigation in the Strait of Hormuz. And because oil is a core input to global manufacturing and transport, supply chains have a natural incentive to dollarize. Indeed, Mideast oil and gas are used to make petrochemicals, fertilizer, and even helium. But the underpinnings of the petrodollar are breaking down due to the Iran war as Tehran exposes the limits of the U.S. military, while the AI boom is sending a tsunami of capital from Asia to the U.S. This time around, rather than Mideast kingdoms recycling oil-trade surpluses into U.S. debt, Asia’s chip behemoths are recycling chip-trade surpluses into U.S. stocks. In fact, South Korean households have 90% of their equity exposure in the U.S., according to Deutsche Bank. Overall, foreign purchases of U.S. equities are now more than double that of Treasuries. “The emerging chip-dollar regime is one where US technology leadership is motivating global savings to be reinvested in U.S. companies — providing funding for the US corporate sector to make enormous investments in new technology such as AI,” Sachdeva explained. Chip dominance begets dollar dominance Just like how oil penetrated industrial supply chain, chips are embedded in the digital economy as inputs in consumer electronics, automobiles, computers, communication devices, and AI systems. She estimated chips account for more than 50% of the capex for a data center. And despite Asia’s dominance in chipmaking, 70% of the industry’s profits flow to U.S. firms. In addition, the key countries in the supply chain of advanced chips are friendly with Washington, namely Japan, South Korea and Taiwan. “The potent combination of U.S. control over key upstream technologies and intellectual property, alongside a supply chain located in U.S. allies has given the U.S. enormous control over chips,” Sachdeva added. At the same time, chips ensure continued dollar dominance in global trade, payments, capital markets, and private sector savings, while also supporting America’s AI buildout, she pointed out. But Deutsche Bank cautioned that the new currency regime has a “circularity” risk because capital flowing from Asian chip hotspots provides financing to U.S. companies driving the AI boom. That means if consumer demand for compute can’t support AI investments, earnings for tech companies would come down—as well as chip demand. The focus on stocks over debt means more instability too. U.S. stocks overall are three times as volatile as Treasuries—and tech stocks are up to 10 times as much, Sachdeva noted. “A dollar driven by chips, AI and private capital connections should be inherently riskier,” she warned. That risk was on display in recent weeks as tech stocks sold off sharply on fears the AI boom was about to go bust. And although Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia on Monday sparked a big rebound, the Trump administration is cracking down on foreign access to U.S. AI technology, potentially curbing the chip trade. Dollar vs. yuan — Coke vs. Pepsi To be sure, threats to the dollar’s status as the global reserve currency have come and gone over the decades. More recently, the proliferation of U.S. financial sanctions has given countries more reason to diversify away from the dollar. But no credible alternatives have emerged yet, despite China’s aggressive efforts to internationalize the yuan. China facilitates its use among firms in more than a hundred countries and across a growing array of commodity markets. Beijing also promotes “China prices,” or yuan benchmarks on domestic commodity exchanges. Chinese banks have more than doubled their yuan lending to overseas borrowers since 2023, and the central bank has reached currency swap agreements with dozens of peers. But Zongyuan Zoe Liu, senior fellow for China studies at the Council on Foreign Relation, argued in Foreign Affairs last month that Beijing doesn’t actually want to replace the dollar on the world stage. “Placing a respectable second, or even a consequential third, would suffice to break the dollar’s effective monopoly and constrain the United States’ ability to impose financial sanctions unilaterally, while saving China the effort and cost of sustaining currency supremacy,” she wrote. “From Beijing’s perspective, the mission is to establish the renminbi as the Pepsi to the dollar’s Coca-Cola: never the market leader, but serviceable in a pinch and more than capable of keeping the dominant incumbent honest.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: DoorDash global food access head: Hunger doesn’t take a holiday. Putting food on the table will take all of us
summary: No single organization can close this gap.
content: Hunger gets harder to bear at the holidays, when everyone else seems to be gathering around a full table. With nearly 48 million Americans experiencing food insecurity in recent years, including 14 million children, millions of Americans will be facing a Thanksgiving table that has less on it. No single organization can close this gap. It will take food banks, businesses, neighbors and public leaders all showing up. At a time when everything seems to cost more, putting food on the table has become harder than ever. Hunger exists in every county, and increasingly often among those who never expected to need food assistance before. More than eight in ten people surveyed by Feeding America identified rising costs as the primary driver of food insecurity. The pressure is building for those in need. Recent changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), the nation’s largest federal nutrition assistance program, have contributed to a significant decline in participation. According to the Food Research Action Center, approximately 5.5 million people have lost access to SNAP benefits since last year. Food banks and pantries have always been the country’s backstop. But now, like everyone else in this economy, they are being asked to do more with less. Organizations are bracing demand rivalling or surpassing experienced during last fall’s government shutdown that created unprecedented disruption to SNAP. Some food banks are experiencing demand levels exceeding the COVID-19 pandemic. Getting food to people can be just as challenging as securing it. Many of those served by food banks — including seniors, people with disabilities, or those without reliable transportation — cannot easily get to a distribution site on their own. Tackling this challenge requires everyone contributing what they do best. For DoorDash , that’s logistics, and closing the gap between food and the people who need it. Through Project DASH, DoorDash transports goods from food banks and pantries to doorsteps. Since 2018, 9 million deliveries of an estimated 150 million meals across the U.S. and Canada have arrived via DoorDash. This holiday season, we’re waiving fees for more than 300 Project DASH partners between Thanksgiving and Christmas, supporting delivery of an estimated 2 million meals. By removing that expense, food bank partners can plan larger holiday distributions with confidence and reach more people. Many of our grocery partners are also doing everything they can to make the holidays more affordable for Americans who are struggling to get by, such as offering discounts for SNAP users to stretch their budgets further. The data is clear: Making it easier to use SNAP benefits can also have a significant impact in the fight against hunger. Since introducing SNAP payments on our platform in 2023, more than 4.5 million consumers have added their SNAP cards to DoorDash, and nearly a third of those we surveyed said it has helped make them less likely to run out of food. This is only one incremental step in a larger national conversation about hunger. No single company, program, or nonprofit can solve it alone. Food banks understand their neighbors and the needs of their communities, and businesses can bring their resources, technology, and expertise to bear. Hunger is a neighbor-helping-neighbor issue. Americans of every background can agree that no one should go without a meal, especially at the holidays. There is enough food for everyone in America. What’s missing is a way to get it to every table. With everyone at the table, we can build toward that together. title: Friendsgiving was named in the 2000s but its history stretched back much farther than that
summary: Of 1,000 people surveyed in 2024, 20% said they planned to celebrate Friendsgiving instead of Thanksgiving.
content: One of my favorite holiday memories is of a Friendsgiving my husband and I hosted in our tiny two-bedroom house in Atlanta. We didn’t have a dining room. We barely had space to fit a foldout table in the living room. I think one of us sat in an office chair because we didn’t have enough seating. But having our friends gather in our home, no matter how small, made me feel proud. I planned the menu for weeks, grocery shopped far in advance, and spent days prepping. As a young adult hosting my first holiday, I felt a lot of pressure to get it right. But I also reveled in the freedom to make it what I envisioned. I deviated from traditional family dishes, made impressive magazine cover desserts, and bought linens and dishware to create a tablescape. While I knew I couldn’t recreate the grandness of my grandma’s family gatherings, I wanted this one to reflect my taste. My inclination to host a gathering that honors the holiday while making the presentation my own may feel familiar. While many people grow up with certain familial obligations around holidays, entrance into adulthood may grant you some liberties from them, or at least some agency on whether to participate in the production of the event. If you’re looking to assert that agency, Friendsgiving is the perfect holiday. As a food studies scholar researching how food traditions are shared and preserved, I am interested in the idea of a holiday that centers friends over kin. I think this is why Friendsgiving, a term that emerged only in the early 2000s even though people had been participating in the concept long before, endures as a sanctified gathering. Not your grandma’s dinner party Modern American dinner parties still have roots in the Victorian era , when a formal gathering was steeped in etiquette and tradition to demonstrate class and propriety and to create social connections to improve one’s status. And while some form of social connection is still likely the main reason for gatherings today, dinner parties can take on many forms, often with the intention of sharing the labor involved. In her book “ Eating Together: Food, Friendship, and Inequality ,” sociologist Alice P. Julier interviewed people of various classes, ages, incomes, sexualities, ethnicities and genders about mainly non-kin gatherings around food. Different forms of gathering require different amounts of labor – sometimes paid labor – and the labor between couples and friends is often negotiated. But she found that women often still took on the bulk of the work in the planning, communication or execution of an event. Within these circumstances, the women often navigated this labor in ways that worked for them or fit their ideas around work, femininity and hospitality. As a young woman, I wanted to emulate the holidays I had experienced, hosted by my mother and grandmother, and was happy to take on the labor involved. However, the beauty of a Friendsgiving is that this labor can be shared and divided in accordance with capacity. Friends who don’t enjoy cooking can provide drinks or snacks, while those – like me – who spend their days scouring food magazines can try out a new recipe. The key is being honest about the time and money you are able to spend and fit the gathering to the needs of the group. No one’s 20s and 30s look the same. You might be saving for a mortgage or just struggling to pay rent. You could be swiping dating apps or trying to understand childcare. No matter your current challenges, our Quarter Life series has articles to share in the group chat, or just to remind you that you’re not alone. Read more from Quarter Life: What’s your apocalypse skill? Finding a future‑proof hobby can bring fulfilment today Five ways to enjoy fashion as a hobby without indulging in overconsumption The ick: The psychology of why a romantic partner can suddenly repulse you A holiday that expands boundaries Today, Thanksgiving is typically viewed as a family holiday. For some, this may be the gathering that provides the warm, fuzzy holiday feeling many search for. But for others, family holidays are stressful. A 2023 survey of 2,061 adults found that 9 in 10 people reported experiencing stress around money, lost loved ones, familial conflict or other expectations during the holidays. As Friendsgiving isn’t an established holiday, participation is difficult to capture. But of 1,000 people surveyed in 2024, 20% said they planned to celebrate Friendsgiving . A Friendsgiving is the opposite of established kin-keeping traditions. It gives the opportunity to gather with found family , and while the reason for gathering is established, the form is malleable. Many people choose a potluck-style as a way of sharing the burden for what can be a labor-intensive meal. Others choose to do away entirely with what is considered the “traditional” meal and showcase foods from their own culture or a cuisine they enjoy. As a parody of a holiday, Friendsgiving gives participants permission to make the holiday their own and be as playful as they wish. So, if I burn my miso butter corn casserole, no one will be disappointed, because they’ve never tasted it before anyway. How to host a successful Friendsgiving While playing with form and bucking traditional structure can be rewarding, there are some things you may want to keep in mind to have a successful Friendsgiving. In her book “ The Art of Gathering: How We Meet and Why it Matters ,” author Priya Parker advises anyone planning a gathering to be specific about purpose. This will help decide the form of the event and whom to invite. Is this a casual gathering with friends? Is fellowship or food more important? Are you hoping to try a recipe your family would never approve? Be specific about your own expectations before you start planning. The Emily Post Institute, which promotes etiquette and offers resources for a variety of social situations, recommends being flexible with the menu. This is especially important for a potluck-style gathering. As a host, you may want to assign dishes to guests to ensure a balanced meal without eight desserts. If you have the gumption, however, you can throw caution to the wind and see what happens. It is also important to keep dietary restrictions in mind to make sure everyone feels included and has something to eat. Make a plan for heating or reheating. The oven is prime real estate during Thanksgiving. You may want to tell guests to bring their dish already cooked to avoid playing oven Tetris. Finally, tell guests to bring Tupperware. There will be leftovers, and I have found that nothing is better than creating a second plate to take home and heat up the next day. Alice P. title: Why businesses are embracing ‘good enough’ open-weight AI—and how geopolitics could get in the way
summary: Rather than paying for the most powerful AI model for every task, companies are turning to cheaper, customizable alternatives for routine work.
content: As the performance gap between open-weight and closed-weight models narrows , a growing number of businesses—from local start-ups to large multinationals—are turning to open-weight models for greater control, customization and cost efficiency. “ Frontier models at scale are incredibly expensive,” Damian Kim, the Asia-Pacific vice president of visual search and shopping platform Pinterest , tells Fortune . “The cost to serve can be reduced dramatically when using an open-weight model versus a frontier model, where you’re at the whims of the API pricing.” Anyone can download and customize the weights behind an open-weight model, which means firms can cut token costs while keeping tighter control of their data. They’re also taking a growing share of AI traffic. In August, open-weight models ran the majority of traffic on Vercel’s AI gateway; 56% of tokens routed through the cloud platform went to open-weight models , up from 7% last year. “Models are converging on similar performance for industry use: U.S. government evaluators put the best Chinese model about eight months behind the American frontier,” says Olaf Groth, a professor of practice at UC Berkeley’s Haas School of Business. “For most enterprise workloads, that is good enough.” Rather than paying for the most powerful model for every task, companies are turning to cheaper, customizable alternatives for routine work. But with Chinese developers behind many of the leading open-weight models, geopolitics may matter as much as cost or performance. The case for ‘good enough’ AI Before GPT-3.5 propelled AI to mainstream fame, most high-performing models were either small academic releases or commercial systems with restricted outside access. The first open-weight models originated in academic research, where sharing model weights to ensure reproducibility was standard practice. In 2019, OpenAI went against tradition by initially withholding the full 1.5-billion-parameter version of GPT-2 , citing risks of misuse such as disinformation, impersonation and phishing. Most U.S. frontier labs, including Anthropic and OpenAI, keep the underlying parameters private, giving users access through apps or APIs rather than letting them download and run the models themselves. In the early years of generative AI, most users preferred closed-weight models because they delivered performance that open-weight alternatives could not match. Yet in recent years, the improved capability and cost-efficiency of powerful Chinese models like Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3.1 Pro and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash has swung the pendulum back in favor of open-weight models. “For the longest time, the idea has been that you can get the highest level of performance using closed-weight models, so many firms start off by using them,” says Hariharasudhan Saminathan, cofounder of Friday , a sovereign AI startup backed by global venture capital firm Antler. But now, “through distillation and other processes, open-weight models’ performance almost matches that of closed-weight models,” he says. “Many of our pipeline customers are now adopting open-weight models right off the bat,” he adds. “They’re not even touching the closed-weight ones.” Pinterest, for example, uses Alibaba’s open-weight Qwen models to power its online platform . “We’ve driven down our inference costs using post-trained open-weight models,” Kim explains. “They offer over 90% cost reduction.” (Many leading Chinese open-weight models activate only a subset of parameters per token, cutting compute and energy needed per request.) Kim also cites the flexibility of these models as a draw. Last October, the firm released Pinterest Assistant : an AI-powered tool that pairs a customized Qwen multimodal LLM with the firm’s proprietary Taste Graph, to generate shopping recommendations for users based on their individual aesthetic preferences. “[With open-weight technology], we can create a specialized model that actually does what we need it to do very effectively, which is understanding visual information,” says Kim. A hybrid approach Rather than choosing one or the other, some firms are using a mix of open-weight and closed-weight AI models. Eu Leong Oh, medical director at The Longevity Suite Asia , a Singapore-based wellness clinic, says he’s using Claude and Google’s Gemini to build the team’s in-house healthcare portal, but plans to pivot to open-weight models for daily use. “For things like prototyping, exploration and research, it’s still very useful to have a large-parameter, trained, closed-weight model,” Oh says. He compares a top-tier frontier model to a Michelin-starred chef. “You’ll want a chef like Gordon Ramsay to decide the processes in your restaurant, but you don’t need him to do the cooking all the time,” he says. “Similarly, within companies, a lot of the heavy lifting and token budget will eventually be taken over by more cost effective open-weight models.” Token costs are also skyrocketing with the rise of agentic AI. An AI agent might consume five times more tokens than a chatbot interface, because it runs multi-step loops rather than a single task. Those increasing costs may push companies to adopt cheaper open-weight models on top of existing closed-weight ones. “Companies are becoming more cost-conscious about their AI deployment,” says Srividya Jandhyala, a professor of management at ESSEC Business School. “Not every task needs the power of a frontier model, and companies are recognizing that ‘good enough’ models work for a large variety of operations.” Harder choices Yet a company’s decision whether or not to use an open-weight model could come down to politics, rather than cost or technical ability. The leading open-weight models come from Chinese companies like DeepSeek, Alibaba , and z.AI ; their growing usage in both U.S. and global business is worrying some in Washington about China’s growing influence over the technology. “The American AI stack remains far stronger than China’s and we must continue to lead,” Representative John Moolenaar (R-Mich.), chair of the U.S. House’s Select Committee on China, wrote in a Sept. 23 statement . On Nov. 18, Reuters reported that the Trump administration was considering requiring U.S. firms to publicly disclose their use of Chinese AI models , in hopes of discouraging use of the technology without imposing new restrictions that might anger Beijing. In a Nov. 20 report, Moolenaar warned that American businesses were adopting inexpensive Chinese AI models. “Federal investigations, however, have found that major PRC developers used proxy networks and fraudulent accounts to harvest outputs from American frontier models and replicate their capabilities. While America is investing billions and racing to build ‘Super Intelligence,’ Beijing is using stolen intelligence to close the gap,” he wrote. Cursor—whose Composer coding agent was built on Moonshot’s Kimi model—told Congress that it’s considering phasing out Chinese AI models due to “geopolitical risk,” CNBC reported . “For global companies, especially in Western markets, there is a trade-off between cheaper Chinese alternatives versus concerns about continued access,” explains Jandhyala of ESSEC. “If they think that future policies may force them to reduce their reliance on Chinese AI models, companies may pre-emptively start using U.S. open- or closed-weight models.” A handful of U.S. companies—including Thinking Machines, Reflection AI and Nvidia—are releasing open-weight models. Nvidia and its recently returned CEO, Jensen Huang, have also championed the technology. According to Reuters, Huang’s support for open-weight AI helped persuade Trump and Vice President JD Vance to push for his return . The concern that Chinese models may come with hidden backdoors may be overstated, says Erik Cambria, a professor of AI at Singapore’s Nanyang Technological University (NTU). “Concerns about Chinese models should be distinguished between genuine technical security risks and geopolitical perceptions,” he says. “An open-weight model deployed locally, without transmitting sensitive data externally, presents a very different risk profile from a remotely hosted API, regardless of the model’s country of origin.” Still, geopolitical concerns may drive companies to diversify where they get their models from. “Europeans optimize for sovereignty and compliance ,” says Groth of UC Berkeley. “In Asia and the Gulf, pragmatists hedge across both stacks and refuse to pick a side, unless they need models and applications which implicate national security.” For businesses, the goal may not be picking a winner in the AI race, but keeping their options open. “Businesses will combine models from different providers and select the most appropriate one for each workload,” says Cambria. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: Global stocks move upward despite shock warning from Panmure Liberum analyst who sold all equities in his personal portfolio
summary: There is nothing but bad news on the horizon, multiple Wall Street and London City analysts said in emails to Fortune.
content: With America offline for Thanksgiving, the rest of the world enjoyed a break from the market chaos caused by U.S. tariff policy, U.S. AI investment, and U.S. interest rate rises. In Asia, stocks broadly rose. Europe was up strongly. And although New York was closed for the holiday, S&P 500 futures were up. Nasdaq 100 futures were up 0.63%, and Nvidia was up 1.29% in after-market trading. None of this should be happening! There is nothing but bad news on the horizon, multiple Wall Street and London City analysts said in emails to Fortune . The most dramatic warning came from Panmure Liberum’s Joachim Klement (who writes a well-regarded Substack on investing whose subtitle is “Thoughts on financial markets by a grumpy, middle-aged German. What more do you want?”) He gave a video talk in which he announced he was selling all the equities—all of them!—in his personal investment portfolio because of the recent selloff in the S&P 500: “I think that we are heading towards a major bear market with more than 30% drawdown risk.” His official forecast for 2027 is that the S&P 500 will sink to 5,000—a level that right now seems unthinkable. His concern is that the index is currently trading below its 200-day moving average: “As Paul Tudor Jones the famous investor once said, nothing good happens below the 200-day moving average.” “It doesn’t look like the Santa Claus rally is in store for us this year” Three factors are driving the gloom: Firstly, inflation is still too high. The Fed’s preferred metric, the index for personal consumption expenditures, was up year-over-year to 3.8% in October, up from 3.7% the month before. “Undesirably strong,” as Lawrence Werther and Brendan Stuart of Daiwa Capital Markets said in a note. That will almost certainly push the Fed into raising interest rates in December in order to make money more scarce—a scenario that generally augurs poorly for stocks. Many analysts pointed to a speech given Monday by John Williams, the President of the New York Fed. He all but telegraphed that the Fed was going to kick the rate up soon: “We must take actions over time that will ensure that we get inflation back to our 2 percent goal in a timely manner and on a sustained basis. There is still work to do to get that done.” (There is a good analysis of the speech by economist Claudia Sahm here .) Secondly, the U.S. economy is strong, so the Fed will feel it has the breathing space to dampen inflationary demand. New jobless claims came in near their three-year low, and the long-term trend in jobless claims continues to point down, according to Thomas Simons and Blake Birkins of Jefferies. “The big highlight … is GDP, which at 4.3% shows that the economy is booming, but unfortunately the inflation data is still too high and is unlikely to convince the Fed to remain on hold,” Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer at Northlight Asset Management, told Fortune via email. “Between the AI angst and the newly announced tariffs, it doesn’t look like the Santa Claus rally is in store for us this year,” he said. Hold that thought! Although U.S. stocks may be sliding, that’s mostly because the tech sector is a fiasco right now. Outside the tech sector (and the outperformance of European stocks vs U.S. stocks is a good example of this), things are going rather well. Before the turkey holiday, 372 stocks in the S&P 500 moved higher, and the equal-weight index was up 0.82% on the day, Deutsche Bank’s Jim Reid noticed. S&P 500 futures were up 0.66% this morning. The U.S. markets were closed for the Thanksgiving holiday but had dropped 0.25% in the previous day’s trading. In Europe, the Stoxx 600 was up 2%, and the U.K.’s FTSE 100 rose 1.77%. Asia: South Korea’s KOSPI was up 0.29%. Japan’s Nikkei 225 was up 0.86%. India’s Nifty 50 was up 0.25%. China’s CSI 300 was up 0.06%. Brent crude rose to $96 per barrel. Bitcoin was at $60,212.
