title: America’s missile stockpiles will take years to rebuild after Iran—and a watchdog warns the Pentagon has a blind spot
summary: The Navy bought an average of 86 Tomahawks a year for a decade, then fired more than 1,000 at Iran. A new GAO report finds no single Pentagon office owns the fix.
content: Over the past decade, the U.S. military bought an average of 86 Tomahawk cruise missiles a year. In the war with Iran, it has fired more than 1,000, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS). That math explains why stockpiles of two of America’s most relied-upon weapons, the Tomahawk and the Patriot air-defense interceptor, will take years to refill. Under current Pentagon delivery projections, CSIS estimates the Tomahawks fired at Iran won’t be fully replaced until late 2030. The Army’s 3,203 Patriot interceptors requested for fiscal 2027 aren’t projected to start arriving until May 2029. A new watchdog report says the Pentagon isn’t organized to close that gap. In “DOD Munitions: Planning and Leadership Needed to Address Persistent Shortages,” released Nov. 19, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) found that the Defense Department has no overarching plan linking munitions production and funding to its requirements, and no office with the authority to carry one out. Fortune reported on the GAO’s findings this week. Why Tomahawks and Patriots are so hard to replace Both weapons are Cold War designs. The National Air and Space Museum says Tomahawks were developed in the late 1970s and became fully operational in the early 1980s. The Patriot’s precursors date to the mid-1960s, and systems comparable to today’s arrived in the early 1980s, per CSIS. The Tomahawk is a ship- and submarine-launched cruise missile with a range of roughly 1,000 miles. The Patriot is a defensive system that can intercept incoming missiles, drones, and manned aircraft, per Raytheon. Besides the U.S., four allies field Tomahawks: the U.K., Australia, the Netherlands, and Japan. Raytheon, a unit of RTX , makes every Tomahawk in the U.S., and RTX is No. 49 on the 2026 Fortune 500 . The U.S. and 18 other countries operate the Patriot, and several other nations, including Germany and Japan, also manufacture Patriot systems. The Iran war, which the U.S. and Israel launched on Feb. 28, drew both stockpiles down fast. U.S. destroyers and submarines have fired about a third of the prewar Tomahawk inventory, and about two-thirds of the prewar Patriot interceptor inventory has been expended against Iranian ballistic missiles, according to an updated CSIS analysis . Transfers to Ukraine had already thinned Patriot stocks. Production hasn’t kept pace because orders didn’t. Recent Tomahawk output has run below 200 missiles a year, though Raytheon aims for capacity of more than 1,000, CSIS found. Lockheed Martin , which builds the Patriot’s PAC-3 MSE interceptor, makes about 600 a year and is targeting 2,000 a year by 2030. New interceptors will be spoken for quickly. CSIS estimates about 1,600 were already in the allied backlog before the war, and coalition partners that fired their own Patriots during the Iran war have since bought more. What the GAO found, and what it couldn’t say The GAO’s public report doesn’t say which munitions are short. It is a version of a classified report issued Sept. 24, and the Pentagon deemed inventory trends and persistent shortfalls too sensitive to release. The public version lays out a management problem. “DOD does not have an overarching plan that links munitions production and funding to requirements,” the auditors wrote. “According to DOD officials, in lieu of a plan, DOD and the services can be reactive to global events rather than driven by total requirements.” The report cites the Army’s push to produce more 155-millimeter artillery shells, which addressed shortages worsened by U.S. support to allies but “was not driven by DOD’s total munitions requirement.” Without a plan that sets long-term goals and metrics, the GAO warned, the Pentagon risks persistently low inventories, or “investing in munitions that are projected to exceed the total munition requirement.” Leadership is spread thin. Each service manages its own stockpile; for example, the Navy’s Tomahawk Weapon System Program Office oversees the Navy’s inventory. A Munitions Acceleration Council created in July 2025 to speed missile production still had no formal signed charter as of November 2026, a senior Pentagon official told the GAO. Service officials told auditors that without a dedicated leadership office, “it may be difficult to realize progress in addressing munitions shortages at any level.” The GAO made four recommendations, including that the Pentagon write an overarching munitions plan and name an office with the authority to carry it out. The department generally concurred. The stakes are financial and military. A plan could guide how the Pentagon spends at least $25 billion Congress appropriated in 2025 for munitions, the GAO noted. Experts split on whether planning or capacity is the real bottleneck “The GAO findings illustrate what everyone can see with their own eyes,” Michael Horowitz, senior fellow for technology and innovation and director of the Defense and National Security Program at the Council on Foreign Relations, tells Fortune . His prescription is to change what the Pentagon buys. “The single most important thing the Pentagon needs to do is continue ramping investments in precise mass systems like inexpensive cruise missiles and long-range, one-way attack drones,” Horowitz says, “because the supply chains and production processes will be easier. This will build resiliency and redundancy into the system.” Michael O’Hanlon, director of foreign policy research and a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, puts less weight on the missing plan. “I don’t see it quite this way,” he tells Fortune . “DoD is scurrying constantly to work with industry to scale up production of key munitions. The issue is less the absence of a single formal plan on paper and much more physical constraints limiting capacity. A better plan might help, but it’s not the core issue or driver.” CSIS reached a similar conclusion in May: With bipartisan support in Congress for munitions funding, the constraint is no longer money but the time it takes to expand capacity and build complex weapons. Elaine McCusker, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute and former acting undersecretary of defense (comptroller), sees both forces at work. Asked about the main obstacles to replenishment, among them factory capacity, supply chains and critical materials, contracting, and unpredictable demand, she added one more. “I would add workforce to that, which is also negatively impacted by the ups and downs of the budget and requirements demand,” McCusker says. “I think two things drive the time it takes to rebuild the stockpile: predictable resourcing to make the most of, and expand, the production capacity of current manufacturing and supply chains and the urgency placed on developing, testing and producing entirely new munitions — and interceptor — solutions.” Her fix starts with the budget. “Fully fund the military budget on time each fiscal year,” she says. “Fund full automation of the Pentagon inventory, parts, and supply system, which is a key component of solving material weaknesses for the department to pass a full financial statement audit, but more importantly, as we see with munitions, it is necessary for readiness and munitions stockpile planning.” What to watch The next test is the fiscal 2027 budget. The administration has requested $1.5 trillion for defense, including 785 Tomahawks and 3,203 Patriot interceptors, though CSIS doubts Congress will pass the full request. Also watch whether the Pentagon names an office to own the munitions problem, as the GAO recommended. Even if Congress funds every missile on time, the timeline is long. The first Tomahawks from the 2027 order aren’t projected to reach U.S. inventories until March 2030, after nearly three years of production lead time. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: U.S. Treasury has an unusual national debt headache: An $18 billion hole from GLP-1s, with families spending $500 less a year on groceries
summary: "On net, we estimate Medicare coverage of GLP-1s for weight loss will add close to $18bn to the deficit by 2034," Oxford Economics notes.
content: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent—and whoever comes after him at the end of Trump’s term—has an unusual new headache to consider when it comes to budget deficits. Investors are usually concerned with long-dated Treasuries pushing up interest rates, or international lenders choosing to put their cash into other assets. But in the era of GLP-1s, weight-loss medications are a new concern for the budget bottom line. Nearly 60 million people will be using GLP-1s such as Ozempic and Mounjaro by 2030, Oxford Economics suggested in a note shared with Fortune this week. This is well above other estimates published earlier this year. JP Morgan predicted in February that 25 million Americans would be using the medication by the end of the decade, for instance. But demand has surprised in 2026, so much so that Denmark’s national bank increased its economic growth estimates in September, largely due to U.S. demand for Novo Nordisk products Ozempic and Wegovy. But with the drugs now covered by government health programs and contributing to potentially longer lifespans, Oxford Economics’ Grace Zwemmer writes that GLP-1s “are an additional factor driving a deterioration in the fiscal situation over the next decade.” Budget watchdogs like the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) have already said the fiscal impact of approving GLP-1s is going to be a problem for Medicare. In 2024, the CBO wrote that coverage of drugs for specific use cases would, on net, increase federal spending by about $35 billion between 2026 and 2034. Zwemmer suggests the costs will be higher due to above-expected demand. More than 1.1 million beneficiaries in the U.S. have signed up for discounted GLP-1s under a pilot introduced this year, allowing patients to access the drugs for reasons other than Type-2 diabetes. “On net, we estimate Medicare coverage of GLP-1s for weight loss will add close to $18 billion to the deficit by 2034. This is roughly 0.9% of the annual deficit, but a much smaller share of GDP, only about 5bps. The cumulative cost over 2026-2034 comes to around $107bn, about three times greater than the CBO’s estimate,” Zwemmer wrote From a macroeconomic perspective, there are also benefits to the government in supporting access to these medications. Zwemmer says that up to 480,000 more Americans could be working by 2030 thanks to improved health. This would contribute a meaningful lift to payrolls and taxable incomes in a labor force shrinking due to aging and lower immigration. Impact on grocery bills Individual households that use GLP-1s could also see changes in their personal finances. A 2024 study by Cornell and Numerator found that households with at least one GLP-1 user reduced their grocery spending by 5.3% within six months of adoption. Most categories saw spending declines, but the largest reductions were concentrated in calorie-dense, processed categories, including a 10.1% decline in savory snacks. The change in consumer behavior is so marked that GLP-1s are helping “keep a lid on food inflation,” Oxford Economics added. Zwemmer writes: “We estimate that GLP-1-using households will reduce their annual spending on food both at home and away from home by a combined $500.” Zwemmer also notes that some of those funds may be diverted into buying new wardrobes, highlighting that new starters on GLP-1s are likely to spend $200 on refreshing their clothes. The U.S. economist added: “Scaled up to our estimate of nearly 40 million users entering 2027, this would translate to an $8bn uplift in apparel spending next year.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: Young Americans agree with GTA VI: Bring back simp culture
summary: In a game built on car theft and gunfights, GTA VI's girlfriend chores get called "simping." Young people say that makes the game even better.
content: Some of the loudest men on the internet say Grand Theft Auto VI turns players into simps, but the people playing it are mostly saying: we like it that way. In a new poll, 66% of Americans who have played the game said its optional chore missions make it better. In Grand Theft Auto VI , you can steal a car, rob a bank and run from the police. You can also pick up groceries for your girlfriend, buy her flowers and help her redecorate the apartment. That last part has set them off. On Nov. 18, the day before the game came out, Braden Peters, the looksmaxxing streamer known as Clavicular, posted on X that the game was emasculating and that “half of the missions are jestermaxing and simping for girls.” A day later, Myron Gaines, a podcaster popular in the online manosphere, posted on the platform that despite strong first-day reviews, this was “yet another example of how political correctness, inclusivity and feminism has destroyed a legendary game series,” and then complained that Jason is pushed around by his girlfriend. Then came Zack Hoyt, the streamer known as Asmongold, who griped during a stream about having to watch TV with Lucia, rub her feet and sit through her friends’ stories, then joked about whether he’d have to buy her tampons too. Jestermaxxing, in the slang of looksmaxxing forums, means acting clownish around women to make up for a lack of looks or money. Picture a court jester tumbling for the queen. In King Lear , though, the jester is Lear’s “all-licensed fool,” the one person at court free to mock the king. Clavicular knows the move himself: in January, a clip of him at a club went viral under a caption declaring that jestermaxxing at the club was the new meta. The complaints spread well beyond influencers. One X user posted a screenshot of a mission called “Flowers for a Lady,” in which players arrange a flower delivery for Lucia because your girlfriend “will appreciate this.” The user then called the game “woke slop” and obviously made by women. One user responded that the mission amounts to getting your girlfriend a gift, drawing in 1.2 million views and nearly 150,000 likes. “Simp,” for anyone who has been spared it, is slang for a man who does too much for a woman. In this case, the offense is a man who does his share. Ben Feder, who ran Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar’s parent company, when Grand Theft Auto IV came out in 2008 , sees the backlash as a measure of the game’s reach. “GTA has always had humor and satire in it. I think it’s always been a part of it,” Feder said. “If anything, what I take away from it is how mainstream GTA has become.” Rockstar Games says the game took in an estimated $3.79 billion on its first day, the biggest entertainment launch ever. Take-Two did not respond to a request for comment. The kids want to simp Most Americans don’t share the manosphere’s outrage. Across all adults in the same Economist/YouGov poll , 25% of respondents said the optional chore missions make the game better, while 15% said worse, and the rest saw no effect or weren’t sure. The split is starkest by age. Among adults 18 to 29, the group most likely to play, 46% said the chores make the game better and 12% said worse. Then boomers, Americans 65 and older, were the only age group where more said worse than better, 18% to 8%. Even self-described MAGA supporters leaned positive, 28% to 19%. The critics also seem to have missed that GTA has always been satire. Kiri Miller, a Brown University professor who has written extensively about the series, argued in her book Playing Along that GTA criticizes the culture of violence it depicts. A game that has spent 25 years mocking American excess is now mocking a newer target: men who think buying flowers is a humiliation. The game has even moved from a series staple: the option to pay for sex work. Lucia, the first playable female protagonist in the franchise’s history, joins in on the action, and there’s now a button that lets Jason hold Lucia Caminos’ hand. Could the biggest blockbuster in history change the culture? That sign of the times might also give credence to what’s so out of reach for many younger generations—and could offer a reason why younger audiences overwhelmingly liked doing chores in the game. After a clip of xQc, the most-watched GTA streamer, went viral showing he spent his first 45 minutes in the game renovating his house, a user wrote on X that GTA has always let players live out what real life denies them, like killing people and breaking the law. In 2026, it’s “having a house and a stable relationship.” William Chopik, a psychologist who studies close relationships, said a game can make even chores feel worth doing. “One interesting thing about video games is that they can take behaviors that might otherwise feel mundane or burdensome and structure them in ways that make them manageable, rewarding, and even enjoyable,” he told Fortune . “But part of the appeal of doing chores in a video game might be that the connection between one’s actions and their positive consequences is much more apparent than in everyday life.” The same goes for love. “Romance isn’t always about grand gestures—sometimes it’s doing the dishes, anticipating a partner’s needs, or making their day a little easier,” Chopik said. He doesn’t expect a game to change young men overnight. “But if the worst thing that comes out of this is that it models more responsible life and relationship behavior (I won’t vouch for other areas of the game that undermine that), I think that’s maybe a win.” That sentiment was repeated by Dr. Liesel Sharabi, Hily Dating App’s relationship science advisor. “Some of the optional missions in the game include everyday acts of service like buying groceries for your partner or fixing things around the house,” Sharabi told Fortune. “I think the game could encourage its players to be more considerate partners by normalizing everyday activities like doing chores or running errands when you’re in a relationship.” Christopher Ferguson, a psychology professor at Stetson University who has spent years studying the effects of video games, is more skeptical. “Despite decades of concern, it eventually became clear that games like GTA did not cause school shootings or bullying or other negative outcomes we worried about,” he told Fortune . “The flip side is there’s little evidence that they cause positive outcomes either.” “GTA6 likely reflects the current culture more than it is causing it,” Ferguson said. “Of course in denying some expectations about its content it’s being transgressive just as it always had been.” Bring back the simp music The music makes the same joke. Emotion 98.3, a soft-rock station of power ballads and love songs, returns from 2002’s Grand Theft Auto: Vice City . Its playlist includes Exile’s 1978 hit “Kiss You All Over,” Eric Carmen’s “All By Myself,” Heart’s “Alone” and Dr. Hook’s “When You’re in Love With a Beautiful Woman.” Exile saw a massive uptick in streams following the game’s release. “It’s exciting to think that someone might discover our music for the first time while playing the game,” Exile said in a statement , 48 years after the song spent four weeks at No. 1. The same goes for Rockstar’s trailers, which leaned on love songs too, from Tom Petty’s “Love Is a Long Road” to the Pointer Sisters’ “Hot Together.” After Captain & Tennille’s 1980 song “But I Think It’s A Dream” (based on a real-life married couple) appeared in an August preview, its streams rose 130,730% in three days. Swedish pop star Tove Lo wrote a new song, “Blood in Your Eyes,” inspired by Jason and Lucia’s romance . And Honey FM, a station of R&B slow jams, is hosted by TLC’s Chilli and T-Boz and plays D’Angelo’s 1995 love song “Lady.” Those songs come from an era when men sang openly about wanting someone, but that era has been fading. Earnest love songs have fallen from 23% of top songs to about 12%. A Michigan State University study co-authored by Chopik of nearly 40,000 songs released between 1947 and 2024 found that both positive and negative emotional words in lyrics declined, while angry words increased. A 2024 study in Scientific Reports found song lyrics have grown simpler, angrier and more self-obsessed over five decades. “But these trends might be suggesting that people struggle to express their emotions, and these songs (and games) might provide a way of expressing things that people want to,” Chopik said. It wasn’t long ago that the sap reached hip-hop, too. In 2008, Soulja Boy had a hit asking a girl to kiss him through the phone, and nobody called him a simp for it. It wasn’t long ago that the sap reached hip-hop, too. In 2004, Lil Jon, the man who made crunk a genre of shouting, slowed down for “Lovers and Friends,” a love song asking a woman he was scared to ask to hug, to slow dance, and nobody called either of them a simp for it. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: A Mark Cuban-backed AI startup is helping families turn Thanksgiving conversations with their elderly relatives into lasting memories
summary: As 81.5 million Americans travel for Thanksgiving, a new class of AI startups are helping people preserve the memories of their aging loved ones.
content: As 81.5 million Americans travel at least 50 miles from home for Thanksgiving, conversations around the dinner table could present a rare opportunity for people to learn more about their aging loved ones. A new class of AI startups wants to help them preserve those conversations forever. Charlie Greene, the cofounder and CEO of Remento, first learned about the importance of recording memories when his father, Don Greene, died during the hijacking of United Airlines Flight 93 on 9/11. A 10-year-old boy at the time of the terrorist attack, which resulted in his father’s plane crashing in Shanksville, Penn., the now 34-year-old Greene mostly has a collection of old home videos to remember him by. So when his mother Claudette, 74, was diagnosed with stage-three lung cancer, he quickly acted to record her memories. With the intention of conducting an oral history interview, Greene searched “questions to ask a parent,” which Google morbidly autocompleted with “before they die.” When he started asking her the questions like “How did you get to elementary school as a kid,” she lit up, surprised he was interested at all. “The thing that blew me away about that experience was how unmorbid it felt,” he said. Claudette is in remission, but her battle with cancer still left Greene “unhealthily fixated” on the idea of how to best preserve loved ones’ memories. In October 2023, he launched Remento, which sends older “storytellers” a weekly text or email reminder prompting them to respond to photos or questions chosen in advance by their family members, such as, “What was the hardest thing you had to overcome as a child?” After gathering a maximum of a year’s worth of responses, the AI converts the raw transcript into a naturally flowing narrative that goes into a physical book complete with images and QR codes linking the text to the original recordings. Greene told Fortune Thanksgiving presents a great opportunity for people to discover new memories or learn new twists on well worn stories from their relatives. “One of the things I want for my daughter is the chance to sit next to her grandmother and hear her say ‘Believe it or not that’s me.’ Thanksgiving is a pretty good excuse to pull an old album off the shelf and make room for the two of them on the couch,” he said. Last year, Greene secured a $300,000 investment from billionaire Mark Cuban during an episode of Shark Tank in exchange for a 10% stake in his company. He has raised a total of $4.3 million since launch. Disney/Shark Tank. Greene said he understands some people’s skepticism of AI, because “A lot of what AI is proposing to the world doesn’t feel actually that good to our lives right now.” Widespread anxiety about AI replacing human workers as well as concerns over its environmental footprint have contributed to some people’s increasing skepticism toward the technology. A March study of more than 3,000 people by the nonprofit Jobs For the Future found that 38% of respondents said AI was doing more harm than good, while less than half said the technology was a net positive. Yet Greene hasn’t gotten as much pushback about the company’s use of AI as he had expected because Remento is using the technology to provide its users with something deeply personal, he added. “Investors want to invest in AI, because it’s an exciting place to be. But I think what we’re experiencing is people have problems and they want them solved, and they want consumer technology to be able to solve those problems,” he said. Kindred Tales, a rival platform cofounded by Nick Hern and his wife Rebecca Hern, has seen a similar trend with their customers. The company has both AI and non-AI versions of its product. While the non-AI version requires users to type out their responses to weekly prompts, the AI version helps by providing speech-to-text transcription and some light editing. It can also write a first draft of the interviewee’s story, if they want. Before 2025, just over half of the company’s customers chose the AI version, but that number jumped to 80% after 2025. “Customers increasingly see AI as a meaningful part of the storytelling experience, not just an extra,” Nick Hern told Fortune . Part of the reason is that the company’s AI chatbot, called “Ali,” gives the interview process a conversational feel by teasing more out of users with follow-up questions crafted to their responses. AI has helped Kern, who also works full time for Thomson Reuters, run the company as well. He said he has used the technology to help filter emails, as well as slowly replace freelancers that he previously hired to help him craft marketing and social content. At a time when companies are spending billions to bring AI to every American, Greene, said, despite its flaws, AI has allowed Remento’s customers’, as well as himself, to record moments with family members that are invaluable. “AI in our company is being used to get people to do things that they’ve always wanted to do but haven’t been able to, and to make that experience as seamless and humanlike as possible,” he said. A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on April 25, 2026. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: Amazon workers on food stamps have tripled despite its record revenue—and it’s just the latest evidence of the new economy of shrinking labor shares
summary: “These are families that are really barely able to make ends meet,” one policy expert said. “And yet they are working, and they are working a lot.”
content: The U.S. workforce has made the type of history it likely wishes it didn’t. Working Americans are taking home the smallest percentage of economic output , 52.8%, since the Bureau of Labor Statistics began tracking the metric in 1947. But as the share of wealth workers take home through wages—called labor share—is shrinking, corporate profits have exploded , with the S&P 500 index gaining 600% since the beginning of the century, while wages have increased just 12.5% over the same period, adjusted for inflation. In other words: Corporations are raking in cash, but American workers are reaping less and less of the rewards. The consequences associated with shrinking labor shares are now becoming tangible. A recent Government Accountability Office (GAO) report found that across the 11 states sampled, Amazon , the country’s largest company by revenue , has 12,346 workers on the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and 11,338 relying on Medicaid. That was nearly triple the number of Amazon employees in need of federal assistance compared to 2020, when GAO conducted a similar report. During that same period, Amazon saw an increase in annual profits from $11.6 billion to $77.7 billion. Amazon’s 2025 revenue soared 12% year over year, from $638 billion to a record $717 billion. Amazon spokesperson Rachael Lighty told Fortune the conclusion drawn from the GAO report is “wrong,” and that it is misleading to look at raw numbers rather than percentages. “When you look at the actual facts, you see that Amazon pay is among the best in the industry, regular full-time employees have access to health care from their first day—at only $5 per week with $5 copays for employee-only coverage—and 74% of our regular full-time employees are enrolled in an Amazon health insurance plan, well above the 65% private-sector take-up rate for full-time workers,” she said in a statement. “We challenge other large retailers to provide the same Day 1 comprehensive health care benefits that we do.” Walmart and FedEx saw similar increases in the number of workers taking federal assistance, as did ride-share and delivery companies. Kathryn Larin, director for education, workforce, and income security issues at GAO, told Fortune the data illustrates that the Americans taking advantage of social safety net programs today are overwhelmingly in the workforce, with most working full-time. The income threshold for SNAP eligibility is about 130% of the poverty line, suggesting that despite many of these workers clocking in at their jobs, they still don’t have enough money to meet their basic needs. “What this analysis really points to is the large number of people who have very low incomes and continue to have very low income,” Larin said. “I mean, these are families that are really barely able to make ends meet, and yet they are working, and they are working a lot.” Diane Swonk, chief economist and managing director at KPMG, recently warned of the hidden consequences of a shrinking labor share , particularly that despite economic indicators suggesting the economy is stable, most Americans are facing an ongoing affordability crisis. KPMG found in February that since 1982, corporate profits as a share of U.S. GDP increased from 8% to 15.85%. During that same period, employee compensation as a share of U.S. GDP shrank from 66.6% to 61.9%. “This chart from my recent Economic Compass still haunts me,” Swonk said in a social media post at the time. “A friend refers to it as the ‘revolution chart,’ which [is] disturbing but telling. Inequality fuels social and economic instability.” How did the U.S. labor share unravel? This trend has been about 50 years in the making, according to Anna Stansbury, an assistant professor of work and organization studies at the MIT Sloan School of Management. Fewer workers in the U.S. are represented by unions —20.1% of U.S. workers in 1983 compared to 10.0% in 2025—giving them fewer opportunities to bargain for salaries and benefits, she noted. But more so, Stansbury blames the fissuring of the workplace, or the breakdown of the employer-employee relationship. In the past, the typical employer-employee relationship would be that of direct employment: A worker for a company does their work at the company they are employed by. For example, a large bank like Bank of America used to employ a janitor to clean its offices. But “in more and more cases, that’s not actually people’s experience of the workplace, particularly in lower middle-income jobs,” Stansbury told Fortune . Instead, large workplaces like retailers and banks hire gig workers or subcontractors to complete jobs once done by direct employees: Companies hire a security provider, which employs a security guard to work outside that large company’s office. Delivery drivers are contract workers, not full-time employees. As a result, companies don’t have to provide those workers equity or benefits. If a subcontractor violates labor law, the company contracting them is not liable. In the meantime, these large companies are not only saving money on benefits, but are also getting to argue that they are increasing efficiency by not spending resources on workers whose roles are not directly driving revenue, Stansbury explained. A bank should employ bankers, not janitors, to get the most bang for its buck, the thinking goes. Brent Neiman, a professor of economics at the University of Chicago, said he believes AI has been the key driver of diminishing labor shares. In a New York Times op-ed , he argued the technology’s productivity promises pose the greatest threat to wages. “Anyone who has used ChatGPT can see how much work now done by people could soon be done by technology,” he wrote. Apollo chief economist Torsten Slok has already observed a correlation between AI adoption and lowered wages. In a white paper published in July, he and economist Sania Edlich found that among 321 occupations between 2015 and 2025, jobs with high exposure to AI saw a 6.7% decline in real wage growth after 2023 (following the wide release of ChatGPT), despite no employment changes, suggesting that while AI is not displacing jobs, it is associated with compressed wages . In other words, companies are seeing increases in productivity, but are using those increases as a cover to raise prices, while keeping wages stagnant. What is the future of workers’ wages relative to economic growth? Stansbury has a slightly different theory about AI.
